title: Weather Station
intro: Read the temperature and humidity and show them on a little OLED screen.

wiring_steps.title: The temperature sensor
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Push the DHT sensor's three pins into J8, J9 and J10: S (data) in J8, + in J9, − in J10. Add a wire from {{pin:DHT_PIN}} to G8, a red wire from F9 to the red (+) rail, and a black wire from F10 to the blue (−) rail.

wiring_steps.title: The OLED screen
wiring_steps.text: Connect the OLED screen's four pins with wires: GND to the blue (−) rail, VCC to the red (+) rail, SCL to {{pin:SCL}} and SDA to {{pin:SDA}}. SCL and SDA are the board's I2C pins: lots of screens and sensors can share them.

steps.title: Read the temperature
steps.text:
The DHT sensor measures temperature (in °C) and humidity (how much water is in the air, in %). The **DHT** library talks to it for you.

These numbers have decimal points, so they're stored as `float`.

**Your task:** Run the code and open the **Serial Monitor**. Breathe gently on the sensor and watch the humidity rise. (In the simulator, use the sliders.)
hints: The DHT sensor is slow: it gives a new reading every 2 seconds.
If you see `nan` (not a number), check the sensor's wiring.
A blue DHT11 or a white DHT22? Change `DHT11` to match yours.

checks.label: The numbers change when I breathe on the sensor

steps.success: Your board can feel the weather!

steps.title: Hello, screen
steps.text:
One part at a time: now the OLED screen on its own. It has 128 × 64 tiny lights (pixels). You draw on it, then `display()` shows everything at once.

**Your task:** put your own word on the screen instead of the blank, then Run.

checks.label: You called display() to show it
checks.name: display

checks.label: I can see my word on the screen

steps.success: Your screen works. If it stays dark, check SDA and SCL are the right way round.

steps.title: Weather on the screen
steps.text:
Join them: read the sensor and show the readings on the screen, every 2 seconds. `print(temperature, 1)` shows one number after the decimal point.

**Your task:** fill in the blanks so the screen shows the temperature and humidity.
hints: The blanks are the two variables that hold the readings.
Look at the lines that start with `float`.

checks.label: I can read the weather on the screen

steps.success: A real weather station! Weather bureaus use sensors like this all over Australia.

steps.title: How does it feel?
steps.text: **Goal:** under the readings, the screen says how it feels: "Hot! Drink water." above 28 °C, "Chilly: grab a jumper." below 15 °C, otherwise "Just right.". If the sensor isn't working (`isnan(temperature)`), say "No sensor!".
hints: Use `if`, `else if` and `else` after you print the humidity.
Set the cursor to the bottom line first: `screen.setCursor(0, 56);`

checks.label: It checks for a missing sensor
The message changes when I warm the sensor

steps.success: Your station turns data into advice. That's what good information systems do!

outro: Your weather station reads a real sensor and shows the results on a screen. You used two **libraries**, worked with **float** numbers, and designed what people see.
stretch: Keep track of the highest and lowest temperature since the board started, and show them too.
Show a little sun or cloud picture depending on the humidity. (Try drawCircle and fillRect.)
Draw a graph of the temperature across the screen, one dot every few seconds.
